title: Tips for Teachers from the Science of Learning
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler reviews Uncommon Sense Teaching, a book and MOOC by Barbara Oakley, Terrence Sejnowski and Beth Rogowsky that translates neuroscience into classroom practice, while disclosing that she endorsed it. She highlights its accessible devices, such as an octopus juggling balls to illustrate working memory and the race car versus hiker contrast for learning speed. She places it in a growing wave of cognitive-science resources for teachers, then distinguishes neuroscience from cognitive psychology as two paths to the same practices: limiting new information, chunking, explicit teaching for novices, and retrieval practice. Her larger point is that teachers rarely meet this evidence in training or PD and are often told to do the opposite. She sees early signs of change in Deans for Impact but notes that with about 1,500 prep providers the road is long.
points: Uncommon Sense Teaching offers neuroscience-based classroom tips in accessible form, using analogies like the working-memory octopus.
Cognitive psychology and neuroscience converge on the same practices, so teachers can choose whichever route they find more persuasive.
Teachers are rarely exposed to this evidence in training and are often urged to adopt practices that contradict it, such as avoiding explicit teaching and quizzing.
Professional development has mostly been a massive waste of time and money, leaving teachers' jobs harder than necessary.
Deans for Impact is bringing cognitive science into ten teacher-prep institutions, a start against roughly 1,500 providers.
quotes: The authors illustrate the limited capacity of working memory—the aspect of consciousness that takes in and makes sense of new information—with cartoons of a four-armed octopus, happily juggling four balls but then looking overwhelmed when the number increases to seven.

Both have yielded evidence for practices like modulating the number of new pieces of information students need to juggle (so as not to overwhelm that working memory “octopus”), breaking complex tasks into chunks students can manage, engaging in explicit teaching when students are unfamiliar with a topic, and having students practice retrieving information from long-term memory.

I suspect that each path can resonate differently depending on the individual. If, like me, you have trouble remembering the difference between the hippocampus and the neocortex, you may find the psychological evidence easier to grasp. Others find brain science more compelling. If you fall into the latter category, Uncommon Sense Teaching may be the book for you.

Either way, though, teachers are unlikely to be familiar with any of this evidence—or the practices supported by it—from their pre-service training or in-service professional development. In fact, they’re often urged to do things that directly contradict what science supports.

The “professional development” teachers get once they’re on the job is rarely any different, and has mostly been a massive waste of time and money. The result is that teachers’ jobs are often more difficult than they need to be, and that the students who thrive are those who would probably learn no matter what.

One promising development: an organization of ed school leaders called Deans for Impact is bringing principles of cognitive science into at least some parts of the teacher-prep curriculum. So far, ten institutions are participating. When you consider that there are approximately 1,500 providers of teacher prep in the United States, encompassing 25,000 or so separate programs

In the short term, books like Uncommon Sense Teaching can provide valuable information and insights for those educators who have the time and interest to read them—and those who prefer a more interactive experience can enroll in the MOOC.
